Why Is There a Gap Between My Gum and Dental Implant?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Noticing a visible gap between your gum tissue and a dental implant can be unsettling — and it is one of the more common concerns that brings implant patients to search online for answers. Whether you have recently had an implant placed or have been living with one for several years, changes in the appearance of the surrounding gum can raise understandable questions about what is happening beneath the surface.

A gap between the gum and dental implant may have several explanations, ranging from normal healing variations to issues that warrant a professional assessment. Understanding the possible causes can help you make informed decisions about your oral health and decide when it may be appropriate to contact your dental team.

This article explores why gaps around dental implants can develop, what the underlying dental science suggests, how such changes may affect your oral health, and when seeking a clinical evaluation from a qualified dental professional may be a sensible step.

A gap between the gum and a dental implant may occur due to gum tissue recession, bone resorption, the natural settling of soft tissue following surgery, or early signs of peri-implant disease. The precise cause of a gap between the gum and dental implant depends on individual factors and should be assessed by a qualified dental professional during a clinical examination.

Understanding Why Gaps Can Appear Around Dental Implants

When a dental implant is placed, the surrounding gum tissue and underlying jawbone form a biological seal around the implant. This seal protects the implant post and the connection between the implant and the crown (known as the abutment junction).

Under ideal conditions, the gum tissue sits snugly at the level of the implant crown, creating a natural and aesthetically pleasing appearance. However, several factors can cause this tissue to change over time, revealing a gap or visible space between the crown and the gum margin.

It is important to recognise that not all gaps indicate a problem. In some cases, minor soft tissue changes occur as a completely normal part of healing following implant placement or crown fitting. In other situations, a developing gap may signal that the gum or bone tissue is undergoing changes that would benefit from professional monitoring or intervention.

Identifying the difference between expected tissue behaviour and a developing issue is something that can only be reliably done through a clinical assessment — which is why patients who notice changes around their implants are generally encouraged to discuss them with their dental team promptly.

Common Causes of a Gap Between the Gum and Dental Implant

There are several distinct reasons why a visible gap may develop around a dental implant. Understanding these causes can help frame a more productive conversation with your dental professional.

1. Gum Tissue Recession

Gum recession around implants — as with natural teeth — occurs when the soft gum tissue gradually pulls away from its original position. This exposes a greater surface area of the implant crown or, in some cases, part of the titanium implant post itself. Recession may be associated with overly forceful toothbrushing, insufficient gum tissue at the implant site at the time of placement, or underlying gum health issues.

2. Bone Resorption

The jawbone that supports the implant plays a critical role in maintaining the height and contour of the surrounding gum. If bone density decreases around the implant — a process known as bone resorption — the overlying gum tissue often follows, creating the appearance of a gap or lengthened implant crown.

3. Peri-Implant Tissue Changes

Following implant surgery, the gum tissue undergoes a period of healing and remodelling. During this phase, some minor positional changes in the gum margin are expected and generally not a cause for concern.

4. Peri-Implantitis

In some situations, a developing gap may be associated with peri-implantitis — an inflammatory condition affecting the tissues surrounding a dental implant. This is discussed in more detail in the clinical explanation section below, and the peri-implantitis condition page also explains when treatment review is advisable.

The Dental Science Behind Gum Changes Around Implants

To understand why gaps can form, it helps to consider the biology of how implants integrate with the surrounding tissues.

Unlike natural teeth, dental implants do not have a periodontal ligament — the fibrous connective tissue that anchors natural teeth to the jawbone. Instead, implants rely on a process called osseointegration, in which the titanium implant post bonds directly with the surrounding bone tissue over a period of weeks to months.

The gum tissue that surrounds an implant, known as the peri-implant mucosa, forms a biological barrier that helps protect the implant from bacteria and external irritants. This soft tissue attachment is somewhat different from the attachment around natural teeth, and in some cases it may be more susceptible to recession or disruption.

When bacterial biofilm accumulates at the gum margin around an implant — particularly if oral hygiene is compromised — the inflammatory response that follows can gradually damage both the soft tissue and the underlying bone. This is the process underlying peri-implant mucositis (inflammation limited to the soft tissues) and, in more advanced cases, peri-implantitis (inflammation involving bone loss).

Both conditions can contribute to the visible gap that patients sometimes notice. Early identification through routine dental monitoring can make a meaningful difference to long-term implant health. If you are considering or have recently undergone treatment, learning more about dental implant aftercare and maintenance can provide useful guidance on keeping the surrounding tissues healthy.

Signs and Symptoms Worth Monitoring

Noticing a gap around your implant is one visible indicator of change, but there are other signs that — if present — suggest it may be worthwhile seeking a professional assessment sooner rather than later.

These may include:

  • Bleeding when brushing or flossing around the implant site
  • Redness or swelling of the gum tissue near the implant
  • Tenderness or discomfort when touching or pressing on the area
  • A sense of looseness in the implant crown or the implant itself
  • Bad taste or persistent bad breath that does not resolve with improved hygiene
  • Visible darkening of the gum tissue around the implant margin
  • Sensitivity to temperature around the implant site

It is important to note that some implant complications can develop with few or no symptoms in the early stages, which is one reason why routine dental check-ups remain an essential part of maintaining implant health over the long term. If you are unsure what to monitor at home, this guide on early warning signs of peri-implantitis can help.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Appropriate

If you notice a gap between your gum and dental implant — particularly if this gap appears to have developed or widened over time — seeking a clinical review from your dental professional is a sensible course of action.

A dental assessment in this context would typically involve:

  • Visual and tactile examination of the peri-implant tissues
  • Gentle probing to measure the depth of the gum pocket around the implant
  • Radiographic (X-ray) imaging to assess the level of bone surrounding the implant post
  • Review of oral hygiene habits and any relevant medical or lifestyle factors

This assessment helps the dental professional to determine whether the gap is a cosmetic variation, a result of tissue settling, or a sign of an active issue requiring treatment. Early intervention, where clinically indicated, is generally associated with more straightforward management.

Patients who have received single-tooth implants and notice any changes in their gum appearance should feel encouraged to raise their concerns at their next appointment, or to contact their clinic if they feel an earlier review is warranted.

How Dehydration May Affect Gum Health Around Implants

One factor that is often overlooked in discussions of peri-implant tissue health is systemic hydration. Adequate saliva production is fundamental to maintaining a healthy oral environment — saliva helps to neutralise acids, wash away food debris and bacteria, and support the protective mucous membranes surrounding both natural teeth and implants.

Chronic dehydration can reduce salivary flow, leading to a condition known as xerostomia (dry mouth). In a dry oral environment, bacterial activity can increase, the natural self-cleansing mechanisms of the mouth become less effective, and gum tissues may become more vulnerable to irritation and inflammation.

For dental implant patients in particular, maintaining adequate hydration is a simple and practical step that supports the health of the surrounding soft tissues. Whilst dehydration alone is unlikely to be a primary cause of peri-implant tissue recession, it may contribute to a less favourable oral environment, particularly when combined with other risk factors.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice for Implant Patients

Maintaining healthy gum tissue around dental implants requires consistent and appropriate oral hygiene, along with regular professional monitoring. The following practical steps are broadly recommended for implant patients:

Brushing Technique

Use a soft-bristled toothbrush and gentle circular or short horizontal strokes around the implant. Avoid scrubbing forcefully, as this may contribute to gum recession over time.

Interdental Cleaning

Floss or interdental brushes can be used to clean between the implant crown and adjacent teeth. Specialised implant floss or interdental aids may be recommended by your dental team.

Antiseptic Mouthwash

Where clinically indicated, your dental team may recommend an appropriate antimicrobial rinse to help reduce bacterial load around the implant.

Routine Professional Hygiene Appointments

Regular professional cleaning and monitoring of implant sites — sometimes referred to as supportive peri-implant therapy — helps to remove biofilm and calculus from areas that are difficult to reach at home.

Lifestyle Factors

Smoking is a well-recognised risk factor for implant complications, including peri-implantitis and compromised healing. Patients who smoke are generally advised that this may affect the long-term health of their implants.

Hydration

Staying well hydrated supports healthy saliva production and maintains a more favourable oral environment.

For further guidance on looking after your implants at home and what to expect at routine maintenance visits, this practical guide on daily dental implant hygiene is available through the clinic's patient resources.

Key Points to Remember

  • A gap between the gum and dental implant may result from gum recession, bone changes, tissue settling after surgery, or peri-implant disease
  • Not all gaps are clinically significant, but changes in gum appearance around an implant are always worth discussing with your dental team
  • Peri-implant disease — including peri-implantitis — can progress silently and is best identified through routine professional monitoring
  • Good oral hygiene, appropriate interdental cleaning, and regular professional care are fundamental to long-term implant health
  • Dehydration and reduced saliva flow may negatively affect the oral environment around implants
  • Early assessment is generally associated with more straightforward management of any developing issues
  • Treatment suitability and clinical management always depend on individual assessment

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal to see a gap between my dental implant crown and my gum?

Some degree of variation in gum position around a dental implant can occur as part of normal healing and tissue remodelling following surgery. However, if a gap has appeared or widened after the initial healing period, or if it is accompanied by other symptoms such as redness, bleeding, or discomfort, it is advisable to seek a professional assessment. A dental examination can identify whether the change is within expected limits or requires closer attention.

Can gum recession around a dental implant be treated?

In some cases, gum recession around dental implants can be addressed through soft tissue procedures, though treatment options and expected outcomes depend heavily on individual clinical factors — including the extent of recession, the quality and volume of surrounding tissue, and the health of the underlying bone. Treatment suitability must always be determined through a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional, and outcomes cannot be guaranteed.

What is peri-implantitis and how does it cause a gap?

Peri-implantitis is an inflammatory condition that affects the gum tissue and bone surrounding a dental implant. It is typically caused by the accumulation of bacterial biofilm at the implant margin. As the inflammation progresses, it can cause the surrounding bone to resorb (break down), which in turn leads to the gum tissue receding — creating a visible gap between the implant crown and the gum. Early identification through regular dental monitoring is important for effective management.

How often should I have my dental implant checked by a professional?

The appropriate frequency of professional monitoring for dental implants varies depending on individual factors, including oral hygiene standards, systemic health, and whether any previous peri-implant issues have been identified. As a general principle, implant patients are typically advised to attend for regular check-ups and professional cleaning at intervals recommended by their dental team. Your clinician is best placed to advise on a monitoring schedule suited to your circumstances.

Could my gap be related to the implant crown rather than the gum?

In some cases, what appears to be a gap at the gum margin may relate to the position or fit of the implant crown itself, rather than — or in addition to — changes in the gum tissue. For example, if the crown has become slightly displaced or if there is an issue with the abutment connection, this may create a visible space or shadow at the gum margin. A clinical assessment can distinguish between these different causes.

Does smoking increase the risk of gum problems around dental implants?

Smoking is a recognised risk factor for a range of dental implant complications, including impaired healing, increased susceptibility to infection, and a higher likelihood of developing peri-implantitis. Smokers may be more prone to gum recession and bone loss around implants over time. Patients who smoke are encouraged to discuss this with their dental team, as it may be a relevant factor in planning and maintaining implant treatment.

Conclusion

A gap between your gum and dental implant is a change that is worth taking seriously — not because it always indicates a significant problem, but because it signals that something has shifted from the baseline appearance of your implant, and that change deserves professional attention.

Understanding the potential causes — from normal tissue remodelling and gum recession through to peri-implant disease — helps patients feel more informed and confident when discussing their concerns with a dental professional. Good daily oral hygiene, regular professional monitoring, adequate hydration, and a healthy lifestyle all play a meaningful role in supporting long-term implant health.

A gap between the gum and dental implant should always be evaluated in the context of your individual clinical picture. If you have noticed a change around your implant or have any concerns about the appearance or feel of the surrounding tissue, speaking with your dental team at the earliest convenient opportunity is a positive step.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
